title: The Way to Preserve Wealth
author: Nie Yuntai
excerpt: The author of The Way to Preserve Wealth, Mr. Nie Yuntai, was a grandson of the eminent Qing official Zeng Guofan and the first president of the Shanghai Chamber of Commerce. inline.s: About This Book:

The author of The Way to Preserve Wealth, Mr. Nie Yuntai, was a grandson of the eminent Qing official Zeng Guofan and the first president of the Shanghai Chamber of Commerce. Drawing on his own family's experience and on the changes he witnessed in the households of the rich in Shanghai, he discusses how a prosperous family may endure and flourish. It is well worth reading, especially today.
This essay was published in the Shenbao and caused a sensation in Shanghai; for a time people from every walk of life vied with one another in donating generously to support students.
Master Yinguang, Liu Yazi, and other eminent men of Buddhist learning wrote articles strongly recommending it.
People took it upon themselves to print and give the book away, and to this day it still circulates widely among merchants in Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia.

blocks.text: Foreword One: A Letter to Upasaka Nie Yuntai (Vernacular Rendering)

inline.s: Master Yinguang

I have received and read your family letters, and my admiration is beyond words. It appears that you have truly inherited Wenzheng Gong's (that is, Zeng Guofan's — translator's note) inner method of conducting himself and dealing with the world. Thus you are able to rise above the habits of the rich and noble, to delight in your own innocent nature, and not to be turned about by material desires. What you wrote in your letter to a certain gentleman is indeed a wonderful remedy for rousing people's hearts and lifting them out of despondency, but I fear that gentleman has no such aspiration, and so it can have no effect. Still, if this letter were made public, there would certainly be those willing to follow its example. If people could, through the comings and goings of wealth that you set forth, go further and understand deeply the workings of cause, condition, and karmic reward in every aspect of life, then the realm of the sages and worthies would not be hard to reach. Your letter is therefore truly a masterpiece for the salvation of the age. From this we know that to make the law of cause and effect clear to the world brings benefits to living beings that are deep and far-reaching. Those who dismiss the law of cause and effect as a mere provisional, gradual, Hinayana teaching are all people who deal in hearsay.

I have often said that to set forth the law of cause and effect, of good and evil, is the best method by which the sages of the world and beyond the world govern the realm and deliver living beings. In the present age, unless we begin by making clear the retribution of cause and effect, then even if all the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, sages, and worthies were to appear in the world together, there would be no way to save the morals of the age and the hearts of men. I also hold that the education of children is the foremost task in governing a state and bringing peace to the world, and the education of girls above all. For more than half the power to govern the state and pacify the world lies in the hands of the world's women. How do we know? That the world has few worthy men is because the world has few worthy women. Where there are worthy women, there are worthy wives and good mothers. Where there are worthy wives and good mothers, then among their husbands and children there will seldom be any who are unworthy. Those who advocate that women must be the same as men in every respect truly do not understand the affairs of the world. One should know that men have men's powers and women have women's powers. To assist her husband and teach her children is woman's heaven-ordained duty, and this power is in truth very, very great. The above are my shallow views; I do not know what you think of them. If you do not consider them perverse, I would venture to ask you to expound and proclaim these principles at length, for it may well prove of some help in restoring the morals of the age and the hearts of men.

blocks.text: Foreword Two: A Practitioner of the Way to Preserve Wealth

inline.s: Liu Yazi

Ever since Mr. Nie Yuntai's The Way to Preserve Wealth appeared in the Shenbao, it was passed from household to household and recited in every home; there is no telling how many people it moved. Yet it is not yet known how many of the wealthy have actually put it into practice. For such things are easy to speak of, but when the time for practice arrives, difficulties are unavoidable. As the saying goes, "To know is not hard; to act is hard." We need not discuss this now; in time it will be made clear enough.

What I wish to introduce to you now is a man of the distant Ming dynasty who practiced the way to preserve wealth. His conduct is well worth studying. In Zhang Dafu's Collected Writings of the Plum Blossom Thatched Cottage there is this record: "In Sichuan there was an official serving as provincial judge who had five sons. To each son he assigned an estate just sufficient for food and warmth, and he himself was frugal in food and clothing. In his old age he took out the salary he had saved over a lifetime — as much as ten thousand in gold — and offered it to make up any shortfall in the public funds. The local officials said there was nothing that needed to be made up. He then had the ten thousand in gold buried in an old courtyard, covered it with stone slabs, and inscribed on them: 'Returned to the Creator.' After his death no one touched this treasure vault. In the xinyou year of the Wanli reign, bandits rose in revolt and plundered all public and private property. Local officials and people alike faced starvation. Someone who knew of the vault reported it to the authorities, and the wealth was used to relieve the people of that place. The lofty virtue of this old man is truly rare in a thousand ages. Even the officials and common people of that place at that time were thoroughly upright."

Readers may laugh at this old gentleman for being too foolish — why bury money in a cellar at all? My own view is that in those days there were perhaps no charitable organizations; he had wanted to give the money to the public authorities, and they would not accept it. At such a point another man might have changed his original intention and divided the property among his sons after all, and no one could have called him inconsistent. For the money truly had nowhere to go. Yet this old gentleman looked upon that sum as he would a venomous snake or a savage beast, and would on no account allow it to remain in his children's hands. Rather than bequeath a calamity a hundred generations long to his descendants, he would ask leave to dig a pit in a ruined courtyard and store it there. Reading this, we cannot but admire his far-seeing judgment; it is truly beyond the reach of ordinary men of wealth. He understood the principle of the way to preserve wealth through and through, not merely its surface, and so once he had made up his mind he would never change it.

In reading The Way to Preserve Wealth, we too should ponder carefully the truth it sets forth. If one reading does not make it quite clear, we may as well read it several times over, until we understand it thoroughly. Then, when the time comes to act, we will feel no hesitation at all. People die for wealth; better to devote oneself to works of public benefit, profiting both self and others — that is the great way to leave a good name to later ages.

blocks.text: Foreword Three: A Warning to Those Clever at Acquiring Wealth

inline.s: Ding Fubao

Every word of Mr. Yuntai's The Way to Preserve Wealth flows from the depths of his heart. A few days ago, Mr. Huang Jingwan submitted the manuscript to the Shenbao; within a few days, readers had contributed more than four hundred and seventy-five thousand yuan to the Shenbao Readers' Student Aid Fund. So great is the power of this book to move and transform its readers.

In the past, Mr. Lu Yi of Taicang said: "Heaven is jealous of talent, and still more jealous of wealth; if a man has both talent and wealth, and that wealth is not what his own lot entitles him to, then extraordinary disaster cannot be far away. I once saw such a case with my own eyes, and so I know this principle to be exact and unerring. There was a man who, within a few years of passing the metropolitan examination, was appointed to high office with his own secretariat and put in charge of the state finances, and he was very famous at the time. His son in turn held office at the same court. For a while the world envied that family greatly. But before long two of his grandsons died young, then his only son died, and then the great official himself passed away. In less than half a year three generations were extinguished, leaving only a lady of over ninety, whose grief was beyond words; she could not even speak when she met people, and could only shed tears. Think back to when this great official was at court: every year he sent messengers to all parts to demand the customary annual levy — a disguised form of extortion — speaking in the most earnest terms, even stooping to words about official appointments and promises. People felt they could not refuse out of courtesy, and most scraped together what was demanded. In this way the wealth he accumulated over the years was beyond counting. In fact this great official had no power to promote or dismiss anyone; he merely borrowed the influence of his position at court and deliberately put on a pitiable air, all for the sake of getting money. Once the money was in hand, whether the matter was accomplished or not, no one could reproach him, and so he could enjoy his wealth in peace. Such a scheme was exceedingly clever — truly a case of talent and wealth together. Yet in a flash he let go of everything and departed, unable to carry so much as a penny with him below the earth. The gods of heaven and earth help those who sincerely do good, keeping it as far as possible from people's knowledge; and for those who do evil in secret, they make it known to all the world. To do good without others knowing is hidden virtue, and its future reward is sure to be abundant. This great official was clever at acquiring wealth and kept his schemes from being known, which is precisely the opposite of accumulating hidden virtue; no wonder his retribution was so severe. Though the old lady is still in distress, and it seems one should not speak of this man's shameful deeds, yet to awaken those who are clever at acquiring wealth I shall write it out as a warning from the cart ahead."

If this great official had applied the principles set out in The Way to Preserve Wealth and scattered his accumulated wealth among the poor, he could certainly have turned extraordinary disaster into immense blessing. In recent years many have made sudden fortunes; whoever wishes to avoid repeating this great official's fate must first read The Way to Preserve Wealth! Those with deep roots of goodness will believe as soon as they read it and will put it into practice; those with heavy karmic obstructions may not believe even after reading, and I fear would not heed it even if the author himself reminded them to their face.

People of this age for the most part do not understand the principles of the dark and the bright, the hidden and the manifest, and think that when a person dies there is no ghost, that all is annihilated. Therefore in life, whatever the matter, so long as it benefits themselves for the moment, they will do it even if it harms others; or though the harm others suffer exceeds their own gain a thousandfold, they feel no scruple at all. Thus every kind of monstrous evil — seizing others' wealth for oneself, trampling others down to exalt oneself, cutting short others' lives to prolong one's own, and all the ten evil deeds of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech — they boldly commit. They do not know that when their allotted span is exhausted, all the vengeful ghosts of those they wronged in life come to demand their lives, and after death they go together before King Yama for judgment; every advantage gained in life, every dark deed committed, must be repaid one by one, whether by falling into the hells, or into the realms of hungry ghosts or animals. The karmic retribution they receive matches the ten evil deeds committed in life in weight and measure as exactly as five sparrows and six swallows (from the Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art

'Fangcheng' chapter: 'Now there are five sparrows and six swallows; they are placed together on the balance, and the sparrows are all heavy while the swallows are all light; let one sparrow and one swallow be exchanged, and the balance is exactly level.' — a figure for the two sides being equal in weight.)

In writing this preface I have set out in brief the facts of cause and effect and of reincarnation, in order to exhort the people of the world. Mr. Yuntai, I am sure, will agree from the bottom of his heart.
Respectfully prefaced by Ding Fubao of Wuxi on April 4, 1943, in his seventieth year.

blocks.text: The Way to Preserve Wealth: Part One

inline.s: As the saying goes: to make a fortune is not hard; to keep it is hardest of all. I have lived in Shanghai for more than fifty years and have seen many people make their fortunes. Of these, some declined within five or ten years, some within twenty or thirty, and some ran through everything in forty or fifty years. I remember that most of the wealthy men who associated with my late father — some officials, some merchants — were for a time immensely powerful, yet today most have withered away and their family fortunes have fallen into ruin. Some were squandered to nothing because their descendants frequented brothels and gambling houses and would not take up honest work; of others, even the descendants have vanished without a trace. Roughly reckoned, among the wealthy of forty or fifty years ago, of those whose property has not been entirely lost, and whose descendants can still study, work honestly, and strive to improve, there is scarcely one or two households in a hundred.

It is not only Shanghai that is so; in my native Hunan the same holds true. Among the rich and noble of the Tongzhi and Guangxu reigns of the Qing — the era of restoration — there were six or seven families holding noble titles, twenty or thirty serving as governors-general and governors, and fifty or sixty as provincial military commanders; today most of them too have fallen into decline. Only a few civil officials' families of modest means are left, whose descendants have fared comparatively well. Among those I know well, families such as the Zeng (Zeng Guofan), the Zuo (Zuo Zongtang), the Peng (Peng Yulin), and the Li (Li Hongzhang) were the high officials with the least money, and their descendants have more often been able to study and to serve society through learning: among the great-grandsons of Zeng Wenzheng Gong (Zeng Guofan), six or seven graduated from universities at home or abroad, and three became university professors; several great-grandsons of Zuo Wengxiang Gong (Zuo Zongtang) are likewise known for their scientific expertise; among the grandsons of Li Yongyi Gong (Li Hongzhang) there are university professors, and most of his great-grandsons are university graduates; and among the descendants of Peng Gangzhi Gong (Peng Yulin) there were, ten years ago, those serving as officials in Shanghai.

Wherever the money of that time came by honest means, and there was no wish to hoard it up for one's descendants, the descendants tended to be worthy and capable. Of the dozen or so civil officials' families that were relatively rich, most of their descendants today have declined; and of the several dozen military officials' families, all richer at the time than the civil officials, with a hundred thousand or two hundred thousand taels of silver, most of their descendants have likewise fallen away; of those able to study and advance themselves, one hears very little.

My family was linked by ties of friendship across the generations to most of the great houses of the late Qing restoration era, whether of the Hunan or the Huai army faction, and so I have some knowledge of how each rose and fell. As for the great civil and military families of Anhui, once far wealthier than the men of the Hunan army, today they have all withered and fallen, too painful to look back upon; in the space of only a few decades, by the third generation, they have scattered like drifting clouds. Yet the few families that would not seek wealth and would not pile up money for their descendants — their descendants, on the contrary, have mostly been outstanding and distinguished.

The clearest case is Zeng Wenzheng Gong. His position was the highest and his power the greatest, yet after twenty years in office he had only twenty thousand taels of silver when he died; apart from the old family house in the countryside, he never built a single room in the provincial capital, nor bought a single acre of land. The Lianghuai salt certificates that he himself created were priced very low while carrying extremely high interest; each certificate cost two hundred taels and later sold for twenty thousand, yielding three or four thousand taels in annual interest. In those days a family with even one salt certificate could be called well-to-do. Yet Zeng Wenzheng Gong issued a special order that no member of the Zeng family was permitted to take one out; for many years after his death his descendants still held not a single certificate. Had they simply used a few trade names and assumed names at the time, obtaining one or two hundred certificates would have been extremely easy; and since the certificates were issued according to the regulations, on the surface it would not have been illegal. But to use political power and position for clever self-seeking — the petty man thinks it does no harm to his conscience, while the gentleman will have none of it! My mother knew the details of this matter very well, while outsiders scarcely knew of it at all. The Doctrine of the Mean says: "What the gentleman cannot be matched in is that which others do not see."

Wenzheng Gong once swore an oath before his subordinates (his colleagues and juniors): "I will not take a single coin from the army and send it home," and for decades he kept that oath as faithfully as on the first day; in this he was of one style with Duke Zhuge of the Three Kingdoms period (Zhuge Liang). For this reason most of the generals and officials of that time were thoroughly honest, and the common people benefited not a little, though imperceptibly. So it is that when those in office practice integrity themselves, they secretly bring blessings to the people; but if they themselves covet money, then every general and official beneath them wants to get rich, and the common people suffer no small harm.

The Great Learning says: "The benevolent man uses wealth to perfect his person; the unbenevolent man uses his person to amass wealth." (One who is benevolent uses wealth to develop and perfect himself; one who is not benevolent uses himself to amass wealth.) Mencius says: "Those who grow rich are not benevolent; those who are benevolent do not grow rich." (The commentary says: "The rich delight in hoarding, the benevolent delight in giving; the one who gives cannot hoard, for their ways are opposed.") For whether or not one covets wealth bears on the interests and happiness of others; therefore to grow rich can create offense, and only by not coveting wealth can one create blessings. The world believes that by piling up money and buying more land and houses one can ensure that one's descendants will have food to eat and live happily, and so people strive desperately to get rich. Look now at the facts of those dozens of families: those who piled up the most money in fact left their descendants without food, and even cut off their descendants altogether; while those who would not get rich by clever means saw their descendants fed and flourishing. Ordinary people also think that without some savings their descendants will at once fall into poverty; yet from the facts of history and the experience of society, if a person truly benefits others and thinks nothing of himself, keeping not a single coin, his descendants are sure to prosper. Let me now give a few more examples.

Fan Wenzheng Gong (Fan Zhongyan) of the Song dynasty had his heart set on relieving others even when he was a poor scholar. Later, when he became prime minister, he took out his entire salary to buy charitable estates for the support of the poor of his clan. He first bought the Southern Garden in Suzhou for his own residence, but afterward, hearing a geomancer say, "The feng shui of this house is excellent; your descendants will produce ministers and nobles," he thought: since this house will bring prominence and honor, better to turn it into a school where the sons of all Suzhou may be educated, so that many more may rise to prominence and honor — that would be far better. So he at once donated the house as a school. His every thought was to benefit the many, and he was unwilling that his own family alone should have the advantage. In the end his four sons all rose to prominence and honor, serving as prime ministers, nobles, and vice ministers, and each was a model of lofty virtue. His sons once asked him to buy a garden estate in the capital so that he might enjoy it in retirement; he replied: "There are many gardens in the households of the great officials of the capital, and their owners cannot stroll in them often themselves — so who would forbid me to stroll there? Why must I have a garden of my own to take pleasure in?"

The young gentlemen of Fan Wenzheng Gong's household wore plain cotton clothes at home. In several decades as a general and a minister, all the salary Fan received was spent in charity and relief, so that his household was extremely frugal, and at his death there was not even enough to cover the funeral expenses. In the ordinary way of thinking this shows far too little regard for one's descendants — yet who would guess that this is the very best way to provide for them? Not only did all four sons become ministers and nobles; they were able to carry on their father's purpose of giving up wealth to relieve others. Thus the great-grandsons of the Fan family also prospered greatly, and the line has come down through some dozens of generations. To this day, eight hundred years later, there are still many descendants of the Fan family around the Fan graves in Suzhou, and outstanding offspring still appear from time to time. If people of the world wish to provide for their descendants, to leave them food and accumulate blessings, then let them act according to Fan Wenzheng Gong's intentions — that is the best method of all.

Next, Yelu Wenzheng Gong (Yelu Chucai) of the Yuan dynasty was the strategist of Yuan Taizu (Genghis Khan) and of Yuan Shizu; most military decisions were his to make, and through them he saved countless common people. Because Yuan Taizu was fond of killing, Yelu, being skilled with words, was able to dissuade him from massacre. Though he was a prime minister, he wore coarse cloth and ate plain food, living most frugally. He was a great Buddhist scholar, and his desire for profit was exceedingly faint. When Yanjing was taken, the other generals all went to the treasuries to seize treasure, while he merely ordered that several dozen piculs of rhubarb from the stores be sent to his camp. Before long a plague broke out, and he used the rhubarb to treat the sickness with great success. He too left no savings at all, yet among his descendants thirteen served as prime ministers over several generations. This is another proof that one who refuses to hoard private money may instead see his descendants greatly prosper.

Then there is Lin Wenzhong Gong (Lin Zexu) of the Qing dynasty, the great man who opposed British aggression and so brought on the Opium War. Had he wished to get rich, it would have been easy enough to lay hands on several million at the time. He held that opium was doing the people the gravest harm, and so he did not shrink from the drastic measure of burning twenty thousand chests of it. Later the British attacked Guangdong and could not take it for a year, but afterward they took Ningbo and Zhenjiang. The Qing court had no choice but to strip Lin Wenzhong Gong of his office and send him into exile, apologizing to the British and suing for peace. After Lin's death he too left no savings, yet for several generations his descendants kept up the family's scholarly tradition; among his great-grandsons there were still metropolitan and provincial graduates, and some remain distinguished to this day. Lin Xiang, chief justice of the Supreme Court, who died a few years ago, was one of them, and a man of most lofty character besides. This is yet another proof that one who refuses to get rich may instead see his descendants greatly prosper.

Look again at those who made great fortunes at the same time as Lin. I can give a few examples: the Wu, Pan, and Kong families of Guangdong all made vast fortunes, several million taels, out of the opium trade. Painters and calligraphers know well that most of the famous old calligraphies, paintings, and rubbings in the land bear the seals of the Wu, Pan, and Kong families, showing that the pieces were once in the collections of those three houses — so wealthy were they. Yet a few decades later these precious objects had passed into other hands. Their nanmu-wood houses were long ago torn down and became ornament and furniture in other households. Among their descendants there is not one of any note. The heads of these three families were, after all, shrewd and capable men, and that is how they made such great fortunes. Lin Wenzhong Gong (Lin Zexu) of that day had wealth within his reach but would not take it, and in the end brought dismissal and punishment upon himself — surely a great fool! And yet, looking at their descendants several decades on, one sees that Lin Wenzhong Gong was the wisest man in the world, while the Wu, Pan, and Kong families were the most foolish of all.

Shanghai has many great men of wealth. Among those I have known I can likewise give a few examples. One is Mr. Zhou of Jiangxi. Fifty years ago, at the Xiao family home in Yangzhou — my wife's family — I came to know this rich man (at that time both families were leaders among the salt merchants). One day Mr. Zhou came to the Xiao house in a fury: he had received a letter from the manager of their Xiangtan branch saying that a famine had struck Hunan, that the authorities were soliciting donations, and that the manager had pledged five hundred taels of silver on his employer's behalf. Mr. Zhou was angry that he had acted on his own authority and given too much. At the time he was worth several million taels, and yet he grudged five hundred taels for famine relief. Later, when he lived in Shanghai, Mr. Tan Zu'an (Tan Yankai, who served as chairman of the National Government and president of the Executive Yuan) sat at the same table with him one day and asked how he had grown so enormously rich. He said there was no other way: one simply accumulates and does not spend. He lived to be over eighty, leaving an estate of thirty million yuan; his descendants divided it into ten branches, and in a little over ten years it was all gone. One branch among them did a little good, and that branch fared somewhat better, though it too met with various unexpected losses and has not much left. By any ordinary reckoning, each branch should have had three million, and they could not all have gone to ruin so fast; yet in fact that is how they declined. If you ask how they ruined themselves, the reader may try closing his eyes and thinking of the ways a rich young man of Shanghai spends money — that will make it clear, and no more need be said. This old gentleman too was engaged in legitimate business and did not take what was not his due; but inwardly he was miserly and greedy, and when famine stared him in the face he would not give money for relief, thinking it clever to hoard and not spend. He did not know that such a mindset runs wholly counter to the good Dharma of kindness and equality. If I hold to the thought of being the one rich family and care nothing whether other families live or die, that is unkindness and inequality of the most extreme kind. Besides suffering karmic retribution himself, such a man comes under the sway of residual retribution — what the I Ching calls 'surplus blessings' and 'surplus calamities' — so that the family that alone grows rich declines with special speed, and the multitude, seeing the retribution with their own eyes, may awaken.

Another family: the Shanghai land king Mr. Chen of a dozen years ago, whose property amounted to forty million silver dollars, divided two thousand each between two branches of brothers. In 1925 I dined once at his house. The mansion he lived in was exceedingly splendid, with a pair of stone lions before the gate such as one seldom sees in Shanghai. In his guest hall the walls on all four sides were fitted with glass shelves, on which were displayed bronze ding vessels, all of them antiquities three thousand years old. One of the guests pointed to these antiques and told me: "The bronzes in this one room are worth a million and a half silver dollars; half of China's famous ancient bronzes are here." These were precisely the words the host most delighted to hear. The psychology of the rich, you see, is to boast that everything they have surpasses everyone else's. But virtue, reputation, and learning cannot be bought with money, and these rich men have no way to obtain them; so they can only vie with one another in clothes, jewels, houses, and implements, earning the flattery and deference of guests who hope for favors. Only seven years after I saw him, Shanghai land prices suddenly collapsed, and with losses from speculation he went bankrupt. The Chen family's ancient bronzes, treasures, houses, and land — everything — was confiscated and sold off by the banks, and the master himself moved back to his native place in the interior.

One more instance: the owner of the Hardoon Garden in Shanghai, about whom the newspapers have lately carried satirical comment — that in all their lives they would not give generously to charitable causes, and that he left an estate of eight hundred million silver dollars. Consider: on a fortune of eight hundred million, even at an interest of two percent a year, the income should be sixteen million a year. If they were willing to take the odd six million of that and use it to relieve the poor, every refugee in Shanghai could be saved. Three years ago there were a hundred thousand people in Shanghai's refugee shelters; reckoning each person's food at two yuan a month, the whole year came to only a little over two million. By last year, when rice was dear, the refugees in the shelters numbered only ten-odd thousand, each costing thirty yuan a month, some five or six million for the year — still only a third of the annual interest on their income. Then consider the poor who died in Shanghai's streets: last year nearly twenty thousand, the year before only ten-odd thousand, and the year before that only a few thousand. Take last year alone, when rice was dear and the deaths were the most: had a few shelters for the cold and gruel stations been set up, keeping those twenty or thirty thousand people alive would have cost only five or six million for the year. To the rich this is no more than a drop in the bucket — and yet that one drop they could not bear to give. A few million spent could have saved tens of thousands of the poor. As for their own household expenses, had there been no extraordinary extravagance, however freely they spent, they could still have saved the ten million or more in interest left over each year. In this way they would have won a fine reputation on the one hand, performed the great merit of saving lives on the other, and still added several million to their savings every year. Such a reckoning is perfectly sound. But they had no such wise vision; their whole mind was set on receiving those sixteen million a year without losing a drop, all into their own bank account, to be their own, to squander as they pleased. It never occurred to them that this fleshly body must die, and that having no children of their own, their property would in the end all pass to others. A fortune of hundreds of millions turns in an instant into a flower in the air, and they carry nothing away but a body full of karmic offense to meet King Yama, leaving behind as well a reputation for being 'rich but unkind' in this society.

They too hang up the sign of believing in the Buddha, but they are wholly unaware that the Medicine Buddha Sutra, in its very opening, has explained in detail the sin of miserliness and the refusal to part with anything. The sutra says: “There are sentient beings who do not recognize good and evil, who harbour only greed and stinginess, who know not how to give, nor the retribution of giving; foolish and without wisdom, deficient in the root of faith, they amass much wealth and treasure, diligently guarding it. When a beggar comes, their heart is displeased; and if they must give, it is like cutting the flesh of their own body, and the heart engenders painful regret. Such people, at the end of life, are reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, or in the animal realm.” Because the very wealthy have more wealth than they need and no use for keeping it themselves, and though they know clearly that many people will starve to death, they still refuse to give their wealth to relieve them. If one reproaches them from the standpoint of morality, this is simply indirect murder. The one who has accumulated the most money and wields the greatest power, and yet refuses to give — the crime of murder he bears is the heavier for it. For example, seeing a child standing at the edge of a well, about to fall in; a person stands beside it, says not a word, does not pull the child back, and lets it fall into the well and die. We would surely say that the child has been killed by him. And the rich man's seeing a calamity and not rescuing is just the same. How much more so when, being so wealthy, he will not part even with a small portion of the interest — then the thousands upon thousands of starving people who die on the roads, must they not be counted as killed by him? How can the crime of killing thousands and tens of thousands be done away with by a mind of arrogance, using belief in the Buddha as a front, grudgingly spending a little of the money he cannot use up, and doing a few good deeds done only for show, and thinking that he has thereby already performed merit and may escape all his sins? I think I fear that heaven and earth, ghosts and gods, would never so vaguely forgive him. So I say this passage of fact is precisely to hope that everyone can tell the true from the false, break open the miserliness within the heart, and in no case repeat the mistake of amassing wealth without giving!

The great Russian writer Tolstoy once said: “People in present-day society, when a million enters by the left hand and they give away one or two yuan by the right, call themselves great philanthropists.” From this one can see that such conduct is a common disease of the world. But for the ordinary run of people it is excusable; for those who believe in the Buddha, it should be earnestly corrected. Everyone must arouse a true heart of compassion and relieve all the suffering of our fellow beings; take the recitation of the Buddha's name and the cultivation of wisdom as the principal practice, and the vigorous performance of all kinds of good deeds — saving people and building merit — as the assisting practice; so that, in accord with Buddhist Dharma, one cultivates both blessedness and wisdom, with the principal and the assisting clearly distinguished. Let me now briefly conclude the above and set it out in items:
1. The wealthy I have seen over the past several decades — their descendants have all declined;
2. Over the past sixty years (this article was written in
), the great families of civil and military officials have all declined, and their descendants no longer flourish;
3. Only the few great officials who refused to amass wealth — their descendants can still pursue their studies and make progress;

4. Those whose offices were highest, whose opportunities for wealth were the greatest, and who yet refused to become wealthy and had their thoughts always on relieving the multitude — their descendants flourished most prosperously and most enduringly; every one of these is attested by historical fact;

5. Of the several instances cited above — the families with thirty million, forty million, and several hundred million — all of a sudden, in a single day, everything was emptied; these were all families that refused to do deeds of relief and goodness;

6. The very wealthy, caring only for their own lavish enjoyment, amassing money to leave to their descendants, and when famine comes refusing to give out a great sum to relieve the calamity, are no different from committing the crime of murder, and are subject to moral condemnation and the sway of karmic retribution;

7. The heavenly principle of Buddhism lies in everyone's heart. Whom everyone thanks, heaven delights in; what everyone resents and is angry at, heaven is angry at. The ancients said: “Pointed at by a thousand men, one dies without illness”; the Book of History says: “Heaven's seeing comes from the seeing of the people; heaven's hearing comes from the hearing of the people.” (Heaven's seeing and hearing come from the seeing and hearing of the people.) The Avatamsaka Sutra says: “If one causes sentient beings to rejoice, then one causes all the Tathagatas to rejoice.” Therefore, to seek blessing, one must create blessing for others; otherwise, neither the Buddha nor heaven can do anything;

8. If the wealthy, in praying to the gods and worshipping the Buddha, burning incense and reciting sutras, do not arouse a great heart of compassion and give wealth to relieve the multitude, they still will not be in accord with Buddhist Dharma.

In sum, the method of preserving wealth must employ a wise perception, that is, a far-seeing vision and a vast capacity of mind. The several figures mentioned above, such as Lord Fan Wenzheng, belong to this class. As for the rest, who are not adept at preserving wealth — the world is full of them, vast as a flood! They cannot keep their descendants rich and prosperous long, only because their own wisdom is insufficient: they can see one point yet miss ten thousand aspects; they see only the surface and not the inner content. To put it simply, when they look at an almanac they see only the first day and do not know that tomorrow is the second, and far less know that at the year's end there is a last night. But though such foolish people are many, there are also not a few persons of karmic roots in society; once a point is made to them, they can at once awaken, and the perception of wisdom will suddenly open bright.

As for what the wise course of action is, please savor the two sayings in Laozi's Daodejing: “When one works for others, the more he possesses; when one gives to others, the more he has.” The several examples of Lord Fan Wenzheng and the others related in this piece are the annotations to these two sayings. Know that Laozi is one of the world's most supreme philosophers. His political, economic, and military learning are all exceedingly exalted, and his philosophy of life cannot be shaken by any age. Among the essential meanings of Laozi's doctrine there is the saying: “The reverse is the movement of the Way.” The gist is that one should turn back — this is the motive for a sudden awakening; most of his whole book is devoted to explaining this principle. Let me cite two more lines: “Know the male, but keep to the female, and be the ravine of the world; know the white, but keep to the black, and be the model of the world.” The male is, for instance, being rich and powerful, and able to be proud — what everyone covets; only the wise person, in reverse, seeks to avoid such dazzling blaze, and exerts himself toward the plain and lowly, to escape others' jealousy. The phrase “be the ravine of the world” means that the multitude will, on the contrary, submit to him. The word “white” means, for instance, holding high office, enjoying a great name, dignity and glory, which others envy — this too is what everyone seeks without obtaining. But the wise person, in reverse, seeks to avoid dignity and glory, exerting himself to hide his brightness, to nurture obscurity, to yield and to be humble. The Doctrine of the Mean says: “One wears brocade but still puts on an overgarment, disliking that its pattern be too conspicuous.” For example, wearing a garment of fine brocade, one still puts an outer garment over it, unwilling to let the brocade show to the outside. This shows that the gentleman genuinely practices goodness and righteousness, and does not pursue empty reputation, in order to avoid producing a negative influence; such a person is the more esteemed by society. These views are all contrary to this worldly opinion. In other words, going against emotional desire in order to accord with reason — such words most people will not take in, or they think it is talking about astronomy and cannot understand it. Yet there are many people in society with wise eyes, and they will surely approve.

blocks.text: The Method of Preserving Wealth, the Middle Part

inline.s: What is the Way of heaven? The Book of Changes says: “One yin and one yang is what is called the Way.” This yin and yang is not empty and shadowy; every one of them can be supported by fact. For instance, where there is day there must be night; where there is cold there must be heat; where there is spring and summer there is autumn and winter; where there is tide rising there is tide falling. Observed from these phenomena of nature, each is one fullness and one emptiness, one waning and one waxing. Extending this principle to human affairs, it is likewise. For example, the one prosperity and one decline of human affairs, one suffering and one joy, one sorrow and one gladness, one order and one disorder. But the yin and yang of the seasons has a fixed standard, unchanging through ten thousand ages; whereas the prosperity and decline of human affairs, following the movements of the human heart, changes without regularity. This changeless change is nevertheless drawn along by the fixed standard of the Way of heaven's one yin and one yang.

Let me try to put it thus: if a person loves pride and arrogance, there will surely come a time when he suddenly collapses; if a person loves idleness and ease, there will surely come days of extreme hardship; if a person loves miserliness and greed for money, there will surely be descendants who squander in debauchery and gambling to ruin him; if a person loves cunning and scheming, there will surely be dull and foolish descendants to be cheated by others. These changing human affairs — a wise person will naturally notice and see them, and know that the principle is the same as the rising and setting of the sun and moon, and the coming and going of cold and heat. The Way of heaven is a diagram of the Great Ultimate: half is black, half is white, and in the middle there is a boundary; once one crosses this boundary the yin and yang lose their balance, and change begins. This is called: when yang reaches its extreme, yin is born; when yin reaches its extreme, yang is born. In other words, what reaches the height of prosperity must decline, and what reaches the depth of adversity must grow.

The great sages from ancient times down to the present have all been able to see into and understand this principle, so they teach people always to place themselves in the position of suffering loss, that is, to be humble and yielding, to give away wealth without greediness, to restrain oneself and benefit others. Among the common run, people without learning are certainly unwilling to do such loss-suffering matters. From the standpoint of the new-style scholars, they would even mock this and call it a negative morality. Know that all great and positive undertakings are brought forth by these persons of negative morality: for only by negatively restraining oneself can one positively benefit others; only by giving away wealth without greediness can one further public benefit; only by being humble and yielding can one be the more esteemed and admired by others, and one's undertakings the more smooth and easy to succeed. In the beginning it seems to be suffering loss, but in the end one still gains great advantage.

People of shallow views and ignorance can only see the surface of all things, and cannot see the opposite side of things. For example, as in chess, they see only one move and not the second or third. They do not know that the affairs of the world are all a game of chess: if I move one move, the opponent must answer me with a move, and immediately a second and a third follow. Buddhism clearly explains the principle of one cause and one fruit, and of response — truly the world's highest science and philosophy. I use chess as a metaphor: when we say a word or do a thing, we are making a move against other people; when we speak and act, the resolve we hold in our hearts is a move against Heaven; all people and all things are our chess opponents.

If we show kindness to a dog, the dog will wag its tail at us to show affection; if we speak harshly to it, it will droop its tail and walk away. As for people, that goes without saying! If I treat others with humility and generosity, they will be grateful; if I treat others with pride and harshness, they will bear resentment in their hearts — and this is still a small opponent. If we bully those who are without ability, or harbour the intent to harm people, or use clever means to take advantage of others so that they suffer loss without realizing it; or, relying on a privileged position, such as being an official or the manager of a company, secretly seek private profit; or, being wealthy, refuse to relieve calamity while comfortably lying at home in luxury — these matters, the multitude can indeed do nothing about, and the law cannot reach him; he has won the game, and his opponents on the other side have all lost. But the Way of heaven does not permit him to win, and will act as the great opponent on behalf of the multitude; Heaven needs only to make a slight move and his whole board of pieces seems to have turned to stone, and in the end he is utterly defeated. This is called: “A man has a thousand reckonings, Heaven has but one.” We are every day playing chess against people, but in reality we are playing chess against Heaven; if we win the greater against people, we lose the more severely against Heaven. Conversely, if we are willing to concede a little to people, and everywhere help others out a move, so as to keep them from losing, then my own game will not be greatly lost either, and on the contrary I shall win a very great game against Heaven!

The Lord Fan Wenzheng spoken of above is the clearest example: he was originally very poor, and served as minister and general for several decades, and yet when he died he still had no private fields, gardens, or estates. Viewed through the eyes of worldly people, he may be said to have toiled in vain his whole life. Yet he won a great game against Heaven, and his children and grandchildren were for the most part noble, flourishing, and talented! The others, such as Lord Yelü Wenzheng, Lord Lin Wenzhong, and Lord Zeng Wenzheng, were all willing to lose the game, and in the end all won a great game of chess against Heaven. And those many persons who were skilled at winning the game, who made hundreds of thousands, millions, tens of millions, and hundreds of millions, were in the end moved against by a single move of Heaven and lost it all. The ancients said: “Man can conquer Heaven, and Heaven's decree can likewise conquer man.” Heaven's decree is a fixed principle of heaven. The law of yin and yang demands balance; when people do things to excess, they have lost the balance. Because our hearts first violate the middle harmony of the law of yin and yang, a reaction arises, and we are disciplined by the law of yin and yang, and made to return to the state of balance. When Heaven plays chess, it moves neither heart nor hand, and yet people naturally lose. For example, throw a ball against a wall and the ball naturally rebounds; the harder it is thrown, the harder it rebounds, and the wall itself has not moved nor exerted any effort nor lost the least bit. So the Book of History says: “The calamity Heaven makes, one may still avoid; the calamity one makes oneself, one cannot survive.” Mencius says: “What you send out to others returns to you.” The meaning is: one creates one's own karma and receives one's own retribution; this is the same principle as the Buddhist scriptures' “one makes one's own causes, one reaps one's own fruits.”

And what is called man conquering Heaven is not truly conquering Heaven; it means that when a person, following Heaven's fixed principle, holds his heart in doing things, in the end he will obtain the later victory. One originally poor afterward becomes prosperous; one originally burdened with anxiety afterward attains peace and joy. Such a victory is the victory of heavenly principle. Although I say that the virtuous man wins a game against Heaven, in reality it is Heaven that wins; know that the Way of heaven can never lose. The balance of the Way of heaven's one yin and one yang is the Middle Way, also called the middle harmony; the Doctrine of the Mean says: “When the middle harmony is achieved, heaven and earth are in their places, and all things are nourished.” If the human affairs of the world lose their peace and harmony, they stir up changes in the Way of heaven: just as the great calamities of war and famine are caused by the injustice of human affairs and the disharmony of the human heart. Strife between man and man, between nation and nation, between party and party — whatever the temporary victory or defeat, the outcome is still mutual ruin; even the temporarily victorious will in the end be defeated. Look through the histories of the nations of the world and you will know that those who won the game were, after all, also losers; and from this one knows that heavenly principle is ultimately just. The inequity and disharmony of the human heart will in the end be judged and corrected by heavenly principle.

Among the humans of the world, the numbers of men and women are forever balanced. There is a family surnamed Zhang whose mother bore ten sons, and a family surnamed Li whose mother bore ten daughters, so that summing the whole world's count, the numbers of men and women will not differ greatly. This proves the justice of the Way of heaven and the middle harmony of yin and yang, with a power of inconceivable, natural adjustment. If we wish to rely on our abilities to violate the balancing power of heavenly principle, in the end we shall surely suffer the consequences ourselves. If heavenly principle and yin and yang had no force of judgment and adjustment, then the numbers of men and women would never remain forever balanced, and everything in the world would forever lose its justice: the strong and the clever would be forever rich and noble, and the good would never again lift up their heads. The world would fall into great disorder, and calamity would descend.

Europeans and Americans observe heavenly principle with short-sighted eyes, thinking that in the world only the strong and the clever will be victorious, and that the peaceable and cowardly should be subdued by others, so they call it “the survival of the fittest.” This incomplete doctrine has led people of the world into pride and evil-doing: pride means having support and so being without fear — I have power and am not afraid of you, and so I put on airs and display my might; fullness means having to use up one's power, and having to exhaust one's happiness, caring only for one's own private profit and not planning for others, caring only for present pleasure and not providing for future concerns. The ambitious aggressions of Germany, Japan, and other countries were led astray by just such doctrines!

The Way of heaven is a very simple matter: that which is excessive is disciplined; that which suffers loss is made up. The teachings of the sages of China — the Confucian, Buddhist, and Laozi-Zhuangzi schools — all repeatedly enjoin and make clear this principle. The Book of Changes says: “The Way of heaven diminishes the full and benefits the humble; the Way of earth transforms the full and flows onward to the humble; ghosts and gods bring calamity to the full and bless the humble; the Way of man hates the full and loves the humble.” The Book of History says: “Fullness brings loss, humility gains, this is the Way of heaven.” It also says: “Only Heaven blesses the good and sends calamity upon the licentious.” The opposite of the word “licentious” is “good.” The meaning of the word “good” is exceedingly broad; if one wishes to define it precisely, all the virtues contain the meaning of the humble virtue, and all take the humble virtue as their basis. The Book of Changes is the book that explains the Way of heaven; the two hexagrams Heaven and Earth are a general account of the purport of the Way of heaven. The hexagram Heaven says: “Able to benefit the world without speaking of what it benefits” — this is the meaning of the humble virtue. The hexagram Earth says: “Though the Earth has its beauty, it conceals it and follows in the service of the king, not daring to take credit.” The way of this line is: to not reveal one's talent, not lay claim to merit and fame, that is, not to pursue reputation and not to boast of achievement — this too is the meaning of the humble virtue. The Diamond Sutra says: having saved all beings, one feels that one has not yet saved them. It also says: giving to relieve the multitude, one is not conscious of having given. This is the world's highest morality, and it contains the humble virtue within it.

Furthermore, filial piety, brotherly respect, loyalty, trustworthiness, propriety, righteousness, integrity, and shame — these are all weighted toward a sense of duty and light toward a sense of right. And the sense of duty is to feel that one still has an obligation to fulfill toward others; this is humility. The evil-doers of the world are simply those whose sense of right is heavy and who lack the sense of duty. As the old saying puts it, to value profit and make light of righteousness is exactly the opposite of the humble virtue. Therefore all morality lies within the humble virtue: setting out from humility, toward parents and brothers it is filial piety and brotherly respect; toward society and the multitude it is loyalty, trustworthiness, propriety, righteousness, integrity, and shame. All people are respectful and glad toward the humble virtue and good deeds, and resentful, angry, and secretly hateful toward pride, fullness, and evil deeds. As for Heaven's sending down blessing and calamity, it is called the Way of heaven, yet in reality it is human feeling; it is called Heaven's sending down, yet in reality it is brought about by oneself! It was said above that the Way of heaven is the expression of human affairs; the Book of History says: “Heaven's seeing comes from the seeing of the people; heaven's hearing comes from the hearing of the people.” The Avatamsaka Sutra says: “If one causes sentient beings to rejoice, then one causes all the Tathagatas to rejoice.” Therefore, when we do good and add blessing to others, we of ourselves receive that blessing; when we do evil and add harm to others, we of ourselves receive that calamity. From this one knows that all the people and all the things facing us are Heaven; everywhere there is heavenly principle within them. Apart from this, there is no other place for heavenly principle to be expressed.

Then, when we act, speak, arise in thought, and show our countenance toward them, we must be especially careful and cautious. Though they may be foolish, or timid, or aged and weak, orphans and widows without anyone to help them; if we bully them, then in the not-distant future I myself or my descendants will likewise be foolish, timid, solitary, and widowed, and be bullied by others. Conversely, if toward these powerless and pitiable people we harbour compassion and moreover devise ways to help them, afterwards I too shall receive others' help, and my descendants will never be foolish, timid, solitary, and widowed, nor bullied by others. This karmic retribution of the cycle of heavenly principle — a person of wise perception can naturally observe it family by family in society, and can even more prove it in the outcomes of every good and evil man in history. This is also one of the most important things in social science!
Written by Yuntai while ill, June 1942

blocks.text: The Method of Preserving Wealth, the Lower Part

inline.s: Last spring (1942) I wrote the two articles, the upper and middle parts, of The Method of Preserving Wealth, and sent them to the monthly Luohan Cai for publication; afterwards, because I fell ill and took to my bed, I could not continue to write the lower part. This spring, through the efforts of Messrs. Rong Baiyun and Huang Jingwan, the article was again sent for publication in the Shen Bao, and was quite appreciated by the readers, and many people contributed money to print it in a single volume; but because they had not seen the lower part, they felt it a pity.

My original plan in writing the lower part was to gather examples of the ancients doing good and accumulating virtue, by which they enabled their descendants to be rich, noble, and illustrious, as corroboration. Lately, in compiling the Memorial Volume for My Late Mother, the Honourable Lady Chongde, I respectfully recounted the excellent words and noble deeds of several generations of ancestors, and in particular wrote the article “The Karmic Retribution of the Meritorious Deeds of the Seventh-generation Ancestor Leshan Gong in Practicing Medicine to Benefit the World.” The seventh-generation ancestor Leshan Gong gave up himself to benefit others, and for two hundred years many generations of my family's descendants have received the shelter of his blessedness and virtue, so it can serve as a most fitting corroborating material for this article. Though this is after all a private family matter, the meritorious deeds of Leshan Gong were once published in the book of the Prefecture and County Gazetteer, and they were moreover honoured and valued by the worthy and learned of the society of that time; the good deeds of several generations of ancestors also have historical material by which they may be verified, and can be said to be enough to win the confidence of the public; they are exactly the evidence for The Method of Preserving Wealth, so to take them as the lower part should, I think, gain the readers' acceptance.

I often examine myself: the time at which I heard the principles of the sages was already late, and the time at which I knew my own faults was already too late. Recalling what I have done in my life, the sins and faults I have committed are too numerous to list — truly I am ashamed before my ancestors, my parents, heaven and earth, ghosts and gods! And now I am already old and declining, and illness clings to me, and I feel even more that I lack the courage and strength to make amends; I fear deeply that the virtue and grace of my ancestors will fall from me, and be lost in obscurity forever; therefore I respectfully record the virtues of my ancestors in order to tell later generations, so that everyone may obtain some warning, enlightenment, and encouragement, to make up a little for my faults.

At first I did not dare to publish this article to the world; it was wholly because friends urged and required me, again and again, to be sure to complete the full text of The Method of Preserving Wealth, that I at last dared to bring it out for publication, and I hope to have something to answer for toward the readers.
Written by Nie Yuntai while ill, April 1943

blocks.text: Appendix 1: The Karmic Retribution of the Meritorious Deeds of the Seventh-generation Ancestor Leshan Gong, Who Practiced Medicine to Benefit the World
(1) The Good Deeds of Leshan Gong

inline.s: My family's ancestral home was in Jiangxi, and it was only from the ninth-generation ancestor Qilong Gong that we moved to Hengshan in Hunan. The seventh-generation ancestor Leshan Gong was born in the eleventh year of the Kangxi reign of the Qing dynasty, that is, in the year 1672. His accumulation of learning was profound and his essays were very good, yet he did not sit the examinations; instead he followed his grandfather in studying medicine, and opened a small medicine shop. Because his medical skill was excellent and moreover he loved to do good and give, his name as a physician became great. Later, because the shop was robbed, he closed it, and even mortgaged the house he lived in to repay a debt, temporarily moving to the countryside. The local officials and gentry, because Leshan Gong, in practicing medicine to save people, met with this misfortune, then pooled money to help him redeem his original house, and helped him rent a room to open a medicine shop.

In the forty-second year of the Kangxi reign, that is, the year 1703, a great plague broke out in Hengshan, and those who sought treatment came day and night without cease, and thus very many were saved. And Leshan Gong relieved the poor and the prisoners especially abundantly. The then county magistrate, a man named Ge, on account of Leshan Gong's abundant virtue and wide learning, specially invited him to serve as his aide in the yamen, and said to Leshan Gong: “You hold the intention of saving people, and I have no way to repay you; let me have your son study and become famous, as a return for your benefiting the world and saving people.” Leshan Gong accepted Magistrate Ge's suggestion and sent his son Xiantao into the Wenfeng and Jixian academies to study. Before long, Xiantao passed the provincial examination as a juren, and subsequently passed the metropolitan examination as a jinshi.

Leshan Gong was then sixty-seven years old, and escorted his son to the capital to sit the metropolitan examination. Passing a place called Shekou, he happened upon a plague breaking out in the depth of winter, and those patients treated by Leshan Gong all recovered immediately. When Leshan Gong was seventy-four, he again led his son to the capital, waiting for an appointment. Traveling north by the Grand Canal, many of the grain-boat workers had caught an infectious disease, and those treated by Leshan Gong all recovered at once. This spread among all the grain boats, and many sick people on the boats called out at the side of his vessel, and used ropes to tie up the boat Leshan Gong travelled in, so that the boat could not move on. Leshan Gong could not bear to watch people die without saving them, so he instructed his son Xiantao to change to land travel, hire a mule-litter and hurry to the capital, while he himself stayed to continue treating and saving people. After several months, when the epidemic had ceased, he then reached the capital.

At this time, Xiantao had just been appointed magistrate of Zhen'an County in Shaanxi Province, and so Leshan Gong accompanied his son to his post. After arriving in Zhen'an County, he instructed the mountain-dwelling people to gather herbs on the spot to increase their income. The next year, after he returned to his home in Hengshan, Hunan, he sent a letter to his son, teaching him the methods and principles of loving the people and administering the region. The words of the letter were earnest and sincere, and when it was seen by his son's superior, the Shaanxi Governor Chen Wengong, it was greatly praised. He had this letter printed and sent to the government offices of the whole province for reference, so as to encourage and spur them. This letter was later included in the book The Imperial Statecraft Compendium, and was recited by the world.

When Leshan Gong was in Hengshan, he often went to the prison to treat the prisoners without charge. When his son became rich and illustrious, Leshan Gong was already over eighty, and yet he still often went to the prison to visit the sick and treat them without charge. The county magistrate, seeing that he was old, sent someone to decline on his behalf; he replied: “Saving people is my most joyful thing.”

When Leshan Gong was eighty-four, his son Xiantao resigned his office and returned home because his stepmother had died, and because his father was far advanced in age, he decided never to take office again. Late one night, when snow was falling thick and fast, the family of a sick person knocked at the door, seeking a physician to go out to a consultation. Xiantao rose and opened the door, and said to the messenger: “My father is old, and in the dead of night it is inconvenient to disturb him; could you come again tomorrow morning?” Unexpectedly, at this moment Leshan Gong had already heard the voice and, putting on a coat, had risen from bed. He called Xiantao into the inner room and said to him: “This is most likely an urgent case of childbirth — how can the treatment be delayed?” Then he put on his wooden clogs and went with the messenger to the consultation. The profound seriousness of this sentiment of giving up oneself to save others is truly admirable.

Therefore Heaven has eyes and sees the merest detail, and the retribution it gave to Leshan Gong was especially abundant. Accordingly, when Leshan Gong was ninety-three, his grandson Zhaokui took second place in the provincial examination of the renzi year of the Qianlong reign. He had seven great-grandsons: Gaomin and Tiemin were both Hanlin scholars and assumed the offices of chief examiner and education commissioner; Suimin and Yumin were both juren and served as county magistrates; Jingmin, after passing the bagong examination, was assigned to serve in the Grand Council; while Zhenmin served in the capital as an official, and Sanmin was selected as a filial-and-incorrupt upright man. The people of the time honoured them as the “Seven Masters of Hengshan.”

On the seventieth birthday of the great-great-great-grandmother, the Honourable Lady Kang, the famous scholar Ruan Wenda of the time presented a congratulatory couplet: “The southern peak gathers the blessing, the southern chant spreads the grace; at seventy the longevity is celebrated, and seven sons have all gained fame.” The wording of the couplet was apt and fitting — truly a beautiful tale among people!

My grandfather, Yifeng Gong, was the great-great-grandson of Leshan Gong. After passing the Hanlin examination in the guichou year of the Xianfeng reign, he successively served as magistrate of Shicheng and Xinhui in Guangdong Province, prefect of Gaozhou Prefecture, and was recommended for the post of intendant. And he held office with integrity, was wholehearted in the affairs of the people, and brought benefit to the localities. Toward the great cases of armed feuds that occurred at the time he dealt leniently, preserving many lives, and accumulated abundant virtue. The common people even established a living shrine to commemorate him, showing the degree of respect he enjoyed.

In private I have often contemplated the meaning of Mencius's saying, “The grace of a gentleman lasts five generations and then is cut off.” The sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and great-great-grandsons of Leshan Gong all for four generations passed examinations and held office; and at the fifth generation, Yifeng Gong too was still able to actively do good and accumulate virtue, and to carry forward the bequeathed virtue of the ancestors; and by the time of my father, the Grand Coordinator Gong, it was even more honoured and distinguished. I myself have the honour to be the seventh generation, and still receive the sheltering grace of Leshan Gong; so it may be said that Leshan Gong's abundant virtue, in blessing his descendants, has already surpassed the five generations of which Mencius spoke. In seeking out the cause, that Leshan Gong's medical skill was excellent and could save the lives of the sick was already not easy; and that with fine medical skill he could moreover make light of wealth and uphold righteousness, and sincerely save people, was the more difficult piled upon the difficult. Among the many famous physicians we have seen in various places, there are indeed many who, by practicing medicine, accumulated a great deal of wealth, even millions and hundreds of millions; but the number of those whose wealth has come down to the third generation is very small. And even if there is the occasional exception, it is inevitably a physician whose skill was exquisite and who moreover loved to do good and give. I truly wish I could meet several more such physicians who do good and save people appearing in the world — that would be the blessing of society! In recent times life has been harder, and the cost of medicine has been high; the poor and sick are mostly unable to afford treatment and medicine — this is precisely the best opportunity for the medical profession to arouse the heart to do good! Therefore I respectfully record here the old deeds of Leshan Gong in practicing medicine to save people, hoping to provide them to the virtuous of the medical profession as a reference for practicing medicine and saving people.

Now I would still like to add some analysis and supplementation. Leshan Gong's medical skill was excellent and he saved many people, yet when his shop was robbed he had to mortgage his house to repay the debt — from this one may know that his financial situation was indeed not good. When he was over eighty, and his son, a county magistrate, returned home, in the snowy dead of night he still wore wooden clogs and went out on foot to a consultation — from this we may know that Leshan Gong remained so poor in his old age! The Great Learning says: “The benevolent use wealth to build up their persons; the not-benevolent use their persons to build up wealth.” Physicians and medicine shops are occupations that build wealth, but if one treats the poor and sick without charge and gives them medicine, one will not grow rich. And yet although Leshan Gong could not grow rich, he was nevertheless able to build up his person, and won the unanimous esteem of society at the time — it may be said that his fame of virtue flourished in his own time and his name was handed down to posterity. Truly not easy! For five or six generations in succession his descendants passed the examinations and held office, and were noble and flourishing, precisely according to the saying “using wealth to build up one's person.”

And Leshan Gong and his son were both very poor. His grandson Zhaokui, that is, my great-great-grandfather, though he served as an instructor and managed the academy and had very many pupils, was nevertheless also very poor. Not only that — I once heard the elders say that when my great-grand-uncle was selected for the Hanlin, the good news, sent by swift post, reached the home from the capital, and my great-great-great-grandmother, the Honourable Lady Kang, was at the time holding her seventh son to her breast to nurse him; upon hearing the news she at once went in person into the kitchen to prepare a meal for the messenger — from this one may know the degree of the family's poverty!

My great-grandfather had served in the capital as an official, and after his death left no property whatsoever; therefore my grandfather, Yifeng Gong, was orphaned and poor from childhood, and when he studied in his mountain study he had to cook for himself. At forty-two he entered the Hanlin Academy. Afterwards he held the post of county magistrate in Guangdong Province for more than ten years; as an official he was incorrupt, self-possessed, and often donated from his income to promote all kinds of good works in the localities, for example: building infant asylums, inoculating against smallpox, repairing roads, building bridges, purchasing burial grounds, and interring exposed coffins. Therefore the savings he left behind after his death were not great, so in his early years my late father had to rely on the wages of his outside work to supply the household.

My mother was the youngest daughter of Lord Zeng Wenzheng (Zeng Guofan). The family rule of Lord Wenzheng stipulated that the expense for marrying off a daughter or taking in a bride must be limited to within two hundred taels. When my mother married, several years had already passed since the passing of Lord Wenzheng and his wife; the three thousand taels of her dowry was also transferred aside and used for household expenses and for making good the money that a certain money house had cheated from my grandmother, until my mother's own savings were entirely exhausted. When she left her home in Hunan and headed east, my grandmother could furnish only six hundred taels of silver for travel expenses, and beyond that there was nothing at all. In her middle years, whenever my mother spoke of those hard times, tears would fall with her words; that she, a daughter of noble and ministerial rank, married into a great household of officials spanning many generations, and yet lived in such straitened circumstances — had it not been personally experienced, it would truly be hard to believe!

The reason I take such pains to recount these trivial, wordy details is to prove the profound truth of the saying that the benevolent use wealth to establish themselves, rather than using themselves to amass wealth — it truly carries deep and far-reaching meaning! What we should note here is this: though this was poverty for several generations, yet it was exchanged for the prosperity of later descendants! Compared with those who leave behind much property to harm their descendants, feeding their arrogance, extravagance, and idleness until their children sink into ruin, the difference between the two is truly as wide as heaven and earth! Lord Zeng Wenzheng gave the house where he lived the name of the Study of Seeking Imperfection (Qiuque Zhai) and even wrote an essay to record it. His intent was to hold fast to fullness and guard against overflow, to remain vigilant even in times of peace! For in this world there is no such thing as perfect completeness; those who are rich in one thing are certain to be lacking in another. Therefore, if one wishes to attain spiritual completeness, it is best to have constant small lack in material things.

By spiritual completeness, I mean that both parents are still living, the family is harmonious, and the descendants are worthy, wise, and intelligent, enjoying the happiness of family love and the joy of righteousness. By material things, I mean clothing and food, carriages and horses, palaces and dwellings, and even official rank and wealth — all manner of enjoyments. Lord Zeng Wenzheng often used this principle to teach his family, saying that family finances should not be too ample — this is exactly opposite to the common view. Lord Wenzheng often said further: the ancients had the saying that the blossom is not yet fully open and the moon not yet full — this is the state of the wise; for once the blossom is fully open, it means it will soon wither; and once the moon is full, in an instant it is about to wane! So-called prosperity at its peak must decline, and joy at its limit breeds sorrow. Could it be that the ancients delighted in speaking these words that sound so unpleasant and unpleasing in the ears of their hearers? No — these words are all truth! And from ancient times to the present, observing the phenomena of society, these words have not been wrong! And they hold without a single exception!

A proverb also says: “no family stays rich for three generations,” and again: “there is no feast under heaven that does not break up.” The wise realize this truth deeply, so when they handle affairs, they first consider: do not seek excessive completeness in anything, and do not let things become too flourishing and go over the top. For the gathering and scattering of wealth they make sound and complete plans; and for their own lives they follow the causal law of maintaining fullness and preserving prosperity; personal enjoyments should not be lavish; and they always bear in mind the poor who are homeless in the streets and without food for three meals a day! Always think of the charitable halls in various places, of the corpses left to lie in the open, of how exceedingly numerous are the suffering people! I should economize my own enjoyments to save the dying and console the orphaned. For a single thought of compassion can give rise to a spirit of harmony and peace between heaven and earth; and as it is put into action, this spirit of peace will often gather around me, and can bring benediction upon my family and descendants. As for these truths, only by carefully studying the facts both ancient and modern can one understand that these words are true and not false!

Conversely, if one knows only to indulge in one's own pleasures, heedless of the lives, deaths, suffering, and pain of others; using deceit and scheming to seize by craft and to plunder by force, and angling by every device — such a person may amass a great deal of money and may hold great power; those who flatter and praise him may be beyond counting; for a time he seems exceedingly lofty and distinguished. Yet the waxing and waning, the fullness and emptiness, of Heaven's Way has its own unchanging principle!

Thirty or fifty years pass in the blink of an eye; time constantly presses forward, and scenes constantly shift and change! What was once a humble lane in cold obscurity suddenly rises to become a parvenu; yet prosperity does not last, and the splendid household declines and fades in a single fleeting instant! For in this world there is nothing firm and imperishable, and no enterprise that can be forever dependable; all wealth and status gained by craft and plunder will surely be squandered and lost all the more swiftly! Only families of filial piety, brotherly love, sincerity, and generosity, and descendants who cultivate virtue and accumulate goodness, can truly preserve their estate and make it great and long-lasting! The records of such events in the annals of history are many, and looking around at the affairs happening about us, they are everywhere! So those with a cool head and wisdom will naturally see it.

blocks.text: Appendix 2: The Guiding Influence of Official Conduct Must Be Valued

inline.s: In recent times the extravagant customs of society have grown very strong, and this dissipating trend can exert an extremely harmful influence upon politics. As to this principle, Master Gu Tinglin, the great scholar of the Ming dynasty, perceived it long ago and once wrote a special essay citing many historical facts.
